newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin calls on G7 to join forces for Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin calls on G7 to join forces for Peru crisis.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday called on the rich countries of the Group of Seven (G7) to join forces to help resolve the hostage crisis in Peru, the Kremlin press service said.

Yeltsin, seeking a high international profile to highlight his return to the Kremlin after a heart bypass operation, sent two letters, one to the G7 leaders and another to Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori.

He suggested that a joint declaration of the "Group of Eight" (the G7 plus Russia) should offer "coordinated assistance in resolving the conflict including possible dispatch there of special anti-terrorist squads from national security services".
If Fujimori agreed, special services of the eight countries should set up a joint headquarters "with the aim of launching an operation to free the hostages".
"The situation in Lima requires that we should show in practice how we are able to act in order to help defenceless people who have become victims of terrorists," said Yeltsin's letter to Fujimori.
The document said Russia was ready to send its own anti-terrorist group to Lima.
The Group of Seven's members are the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Japan.

Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told a Kremlin briefing that both documents had been sent several hours ago. He declined to say whether the 65-year-old Kremlin leader had discussed his proposal with G7 leaders.

The Russian president said in his letter the seizure of hostages in Peru proved that terrorism did not have national boundaries, a clear reference to Moscow's battle against what it has called "Chechen terrorism".

Russia's special services, especially the Federal Security Service, has suffered a series of public setbacks during Moscow's 21-month abortive attempt to bring Chechen separatists to heel by military methods.
"Our experience, especially in the Chechen republic, showed that Russia always favoured peaceful resolution of crises through talks," Yastrzhembsky said.
"But when the reserve of politcal action is exhausted, there emerges a neccessity for consolidated action."

Rebels belonging to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement seized hundreds of hostages at a Japanese embassy reception in the Peruvian capital last Tuesday. More than 100 of them, including six ambassadors, are still in their hands.
